amendments.rule: **A verb the ASV renders as a light verb plus a complement heads on the complement, not on the light verb.** This is rule 31's test applied to a verb: drop each word in turn, and the head is the one whose loss loses the lexeme. `הַאֲזִין` → *Give ear unto* heads on *ear*, because *give* alone gives anything; so too `הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה` → *did obeisance*, `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel*, `הִמְלִיךְ` → *make king*, `הוֹדָה` → *give thanks*, `כִּלָּה` → *made an end*, `עוּד` → *bear witness*, `חָנַן` → *make supplication*, `בּוֹשׁ` → *put to shame*. The complement need not be a noun: an adjective (`הִכְבִּיד` → *made heavy*, `גָּדַל` → *make greater*) and a second verb (`חָטָא` hiphil → *made to sin*, `אָכַל` → *did eat*) are read the same way. Rule 24's *lexical predicate over subjects and auxiliaries* is about `was gathered`, and must not be read as a preference for the English verb — that reasoning would head *make king* on *make*. **A phrasal particle is not a complement.** `שָׁלַח` → *put forth*, `סוּר` → *take away*, and `נָתַן` → *put away* are one lexical verb plus its particle, and the head stays on the verb; the same subtraction says so, since *forth* and *away* alone name nothing. **A supplied object is not a complement either, and that holds of any verb's rendering and not only a light verb's.** Where the ASV writes an object pronoun inside or beside a Hebrew verb's rendering — `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let* ***it*** *fall*, `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave* ***them*** *drink*, `אֲנִי שָׁמָעְתִּי` → *I have heard* ***it*** — read whether an object morpheme is present. Where one is, it takes the pronoun under rule 18 and the verb keeps the rest, as in `וַיַּעֲבִירֵם` → *caused* ***them*** *to pass through*. Where none is, the pronoun answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside or beside its rendering; rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing the verb's own person and number, which is a subject, and never an object the Hebrew does not write, exactly as that rule leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added`. The verb's unit is discontinuous around such a pronoun under rule 25. **This applies only to a pronoun that truly supplies an object.** A reflexive pronoun the ASV uses to render the Hebrew verb's own voice or its elative sense is part of that verb's unit, because the source verb licenses it: `אִכַּף` → *bow myself* keeps *myself* with the Niphal verb and heads on *bow*, and `הִגְדִּיל עַל` → *magnified yourselves against* keeps *yourselves* with the Hiphil on the same ground. Position inside the English verb phrase is not what makes a word part of the verb's rendering — the complement, or the source verb's own voice or sense, must license it, and an unsupported object does not. **But a preposition the ASV supplies to reach the verb's own object is part of that rendering.** Where the Hebrew writes a bare direct object — no object marker on it and no preposition of its own — and the English verb reaches that object through a preposition the ASV has written, the preposition belongs to the verb's unit and not to the object noun's: `חָמְסוּ תוֹרָתִי` → *have done violence* ***to*** *my law*, `תְּבַצְּעִי רֵעַיִךְ` → *hast greedily gained* ***of*** *thy neighbors*, `הֵקַלּוּ אָב וָאֵם` → *have set light* ***by*** *father and mother*, `אֲבַקֵּשׁ אִישׁ` → *sought* ***for*** *a man*, `טָחוּ תָּפֵל` → *have daubed ... with untempered mortar*. This is rule 16's reasoning where no marker stands to take the word: the same subtraction test finds that dropping it diminishes nothing but the object relation, and the object noun's own English is the noun. The unit is discontinuous under rule 25 where other material stands between the verb and the preposition, and the head is unaffected — it stays on the lexical verb, or on the complement where this rule's light-verb clause puts it. **And the object so reached may be a pronominal suffix on the verb rather than a noun.** Where a verbal object suffix stands with no preposition of its own and the English rendering reaches it through a supplied preposition — `יִבְּמָהּ` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *her*, `יַבְּמִי` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *me* — that preposition belongs to the verb's unit on exactly the terms just given, and the suffix keeps only the pronoun rule 18 writes for it. Do not read rule 18's *the English pronoun that realizes it* as reaching the preposition standing beside that pronoun: what that rule places is the pronoun, and a preposition the English verb's valency licenses is the verb's whether its object is a noun or a suffix. Rule 40 does not reach such a suffix either, since no preposition morpheme stands in the clause for the recasting to silence. Test by subtraction as before — drop the English preposition and ask whether anything but the object relation is diminished. Two limits. Where an object marker or a preposition of the object's own is present, that morpheme takes the word under rules 16 and 11, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And this does not touch rule 33: a function word supplied for an adverbial accusative is licensed by that noun's own case-function and stays with the noun, whereas a word supplied for a direct object is licensed by the English verb's valency, so read which the Hebrew noun is before placing it.
amendments.why: The supplied-preposition clause was written for a bare object noun and says *the object noun's*, so it did not on its face reach a verbal object suffix. DEU.25.5 (`יִבְּמָהּ` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother unto her*) and DEU.25.7 (`יַבְּמִי` → *... unto me*) were both first aligned by giving the *unto* to the suffix under rule 18 and both had to be corrected — the rule meeting a case it had not considered. The amendment widens the existing clause in place rather than adding a cross-referencing rule, keeps its subtraction test and both of its limits verbatim, and states the boundary against rules 18 and 40 that the corrections turned on. It contradicts nothing in the corpus: rule 18 still places the pronoun, and rule 40 still governs a preposition morpheme the recasting silences, which is absent here.

conventions: לְ before a construct body-part noun is fused or split by what the ASV writes for the pair, and this chapter writes both shapes: `לְעֵינֶיךָ` → *unto thee* (25.3) is one unit on the preposition and עַיִן, headed on the construct noun under rule 23, while `לְפָנָיו` → *before his face* (25.2) and `לְעֵינֵי` → *in the presence of* (25.9) are split under rule 2, each morpheme holding the word written for it. The suffix keeps its own pronoun in all three, and the construct noun is never marked `unrepresented` beside a preposition holding the whole English word.

The levirate verb יָבַם is rendered by a light verb plus complement — *perform the duty of a husband's brother* — headed on *duty*, which is the word whose loss loses the lexeme; *brother* was the competing head and is named in both verse notes. The supplied *unto* by which that English phrase reaches the verb's object suffix belongs to the verb's unit and the suffix keeps only its pronoun (25.5, 25.7).

The distributive doubled noun `אֶבֶן וָאֶבֶן` / `אֵיפָה וְאֵיפָה` → *diverse weights* / *diverse measures* is one `noncompositional` unit across both nouns and the waw, headed on the first noun under rule 6's deterministic anchor and on the English noun. The competing split — the first noun taking *weights*, *diverse* going to the waw, the second noun `unrepresented` — was rejected because no morpheme owns *diverse* in particular and assigning it to the conjunction is arbitrary (25.13, 25.14).

A possessive clause built on the negative existential is rule 43's verbless case, not rule 50's frame: `אֵין־לוֹ` → *have no son* gives *no* to אַיִן, which heads on the negation word, and *have* to the possessive לְ, which is what makes the clause possessive (25.5). Where הָיָה is written instead, the verb takes the *have* itself and the לְ is `unrepresented` (25.13, 25.14, 25.15 twice). The suffix takes the subject pronoun in either shape unless the ASV carries the subject over from a preceding clause, as at 25.5.

report: Read all 35 candidate groups and then the dump end to end, since the table is keyed by source lemma and cannot see `added` units. No genuine cross-verse split: every multi-treatment bucket is a difference the ASV writes and the source licenses.

לְ before a construct body-part noun is the chapter's main recurring shape and is consistent. `לְפָנָיו` → *before his face* (25.2) and `לְעֵינֵי` → *in the presence of* (25.9) split under rule 2 because the ASV spends a word on each morpheme; `לְעֵינֶיךָ` → *unto thee* (25.3) fuses on עַיִן under rule 30 because it spends one. 25.3 records that correction.

The three הָיָה frames divide as rule 45 directs, read off the Hebrew each time: the frame's *that* is on the apodosis waw at 25.2, where וְהִפִּילוֹ opens the apodosis, and on the verb at 25.6 and 25.19, where the apodosis carries no waw of its own.

Possessive clauses cover both of rule 43's cases and agree with it. הָיָה takes the *have* and leaves its לְ `unrepresented` at 25.13, 25.14 and twice at 25.15; the verbless `אֵין־לוֹ` at 25.5 gives *no* to אַיִן and *have* to the possessive לְ, the suffix `unrepresented` because the ASV carries the subject over from the preceding clause.

The two levirate verbs (25.5 יִבְּמָהּ, 25.7 יַבְּמִי) agree, each after a recorded correction: the light-verb rendering heads on *duty* and the supplied *unto* joins the verb's unit while the suffix keeps its pronoun. Rule 44's supplied-preposition clause names only an object noun, which is why both verse passes first misplaced it; it is amended below to reach a verbal object suffix.

The five `added` units — *the judges* (25.1), *if* and *and* (25.3), *the grain* (25.4), *even* (25.16) — are each a supplied word no morpheme answers to, and nowhere else in the chapter is a comparable supplied word folded into a neighbouring rendering. All seven object markers are `unrepresented`, and the doubled-noun idiom is read identically at 25.13 and 25.14.

BSB: no genuine error among the 14 disagreements. Every one is the documented convention difference — an article the ASV writes no *the* for (rule 29), a suffix the ASV leaves unrendered (rule 22), or a preposition a recasting silences (rules 40, 43, 52). BSB attaches each to its host phrase; none would change on direct analysis of the Hebrew, and no accepted edge was touched.

Declined to promote the distributive doubled-noun idiom (`אֶבֶן וָאֶבֶן` → *diverse weights*). The briefing shows no corpus precedent for how finished chapters read such a repetition, and rules 22 and 30 pull opposite ways on the waw; the chapter's reading and its competing split are recorded as a convention instead of a rule the corpus might contradict.
